signals.title: Outstanding Almansa eases to fourth victory of 2026 with dominant Lusail display
signals.summary: A lights to flag victory for the 20-year-old sees him connect 4 this season whilst Fernandez pips Quiles for P2 Taking his most dominant and comfortable win yet, David Almansa (Liqui Moly Dynavolt Intact GP) snatched the holeshot at Turn 1 and never looked back. Win number four for 2026 and a mighty display saw him pull clear and finish 2.5 seconds clear of ex-teammate Adrian Fernandez (Leopard Racing) in second and World Champion Maximo Quiles (CFMOTO Gaviota Aspar Team) in third. Taking 14th after a collision and crash early on, Brian Uriarte (Red Bull KTM Ajo) has wrapped up the Rookie of the Year title in Moto3. Holeshot honours went the way of Almansa who got a great launch from second on the grid. Polesitter Quiles dropped to P3 behind Uriarte before being beaten back to seventh by the end of Lap 1 by Fernandez, David Muñoz (Liqui Moly Dynavolt Intact GP), Alvaro Carpe (Red Bull KTM Ajo) and Rico Salmela (Red Bull KTM Tech3). The Champion recovered into the top five by the start of Lap 2 but at Turn 1, contact between Muñoz and Uriarte left the latter on the floor. For causing the crash, Muñoz was handed a Long Lap Penalty. Avoiding all the fighting behind, Almansa began to stretch his legs and by Lap 3 had a second over Quiles but the Champion was already starting to hunt down the #22, bring Fernandez and Carpe with him. By Lap 6, the gap was hovering at 1.2s but behind, Muñoz had got himself in more trouble, this time for taking out Eddie O’Shea at Turn 14 and therefore being given a double Long Lap Penalty. At half GP distance, Almansa and Quiles were matching each other with Fernandez clinging on whereas Carpe couldn’t stay with the podium battle and had dropped back into the chasing pack of Joel Kelso (Gryd Racing) and Veda Pratama (Honda Team Asia). With the #22 clear off out front into the closing stages, it was tight for P2 as Fernandez piled on the pressure to Quiles, eventually seeing the World Champion make a rare mistake at Turn 6 with two and a half laps to go. The #31 got into P2 but Quiles hadn’t given up the fight just yet. Try as he might though, Fernandez had too much going into the final lap. At the front of the field, Almansa was cruising to another victory, a fourth of the season and looking to put one hand on the silver medal for 2026. Victory at the chequered flag and leading every single lap from start to finish and going unchallenged, it was one of the #22’s best yet. Fernandez resisted Quiles’ late charge to the line by 0.069s and whilst P3 left the Spaniard wanting more, it was enough to wrap up the Teams’ Championship for the year. Behind, Pratama overcame Carpe whilst Kelso, Hakim Danish (AEON Credit – MT Helmets – MSI), Muñoz, Ryusei Yamanaka (AEON Credit – MT Helmets – MSI) and Scott Ogden (CIP GreenPower) rounded out the top ten. Uriarte recovered to pick up two points, enough to give him the Rookie of the Year accolade for 2026. Two rounds to go, Almansa can secure P2 overall next time out with a top four finish at Portimao; don’t miss it! signals.title: Luca Marini withdraws from Qatar GP
signals.summary: The Honda HRC Castrol rider will miss the Sunday Grand Prix at Lusail due to fatigue After Warm Up at the Lusail International Circuit, Luca Marini and the Honda HRC Castrol team announced they have elected to withdraw from the Qatar GP due to his ongoing state of fatigue, and to focus on the final two rounds of the 2026 MotoGP World Championship. The Italian rider, who qualified 14 th on the grid and finished 13 th in Saturday’s Sprint at Lusail, completed four full laps of Sunday morning’s Warm Up in Qatar. We wish Marini and his team all the best and hope to see them back racing in Portimao on November 20 th . The Season Finale is now streaming, don’t miss anything with MotoGP™ VideoPass

signals.title: Holgado powers clear for victory as Guevara DNFs in Qatar
signals.summary: The Aspar star produces unreal late-race pace to clinch a second win of 2026; Ortola and Escrig claim podiums while Gonzalez extends his championship lead to 13.5 points Some unbeatable late-race pace from MotoGP-bound Daniel Holgado (CFMOTO Power Electronics Aspar Team) saw the #96 power to a second victory of the season by 2.2s at the Qatar Airways Grand Prix of Qatar, as Ivan Ortola (QJMOTOR – MSI) - from P14 on the grid - and polesitter Alex Escrig (KLINT Racing Team) treat us to a tight fight for P2 that was won on the run to the line by the rider third in the standings. Meanwhile, in the championship chase, drama unfolded. Izan Guevara (BLU CRU Pramac Yamaha Moto2) suffered a problem with his bike to see the Spaniard suffer his first DNF since the 2025 Japanese GP, and with Manuel Gonzalez (Liqui Moly Dynavolt Intact GP) finishing P6, it means the gap between the pair sits at 13.5 points with two to go. Match point ManuGas in Portimao. From lights out, Gonzalez got a great launch from the middle of the second row to immediately climb into P3, as Collin Veijer (Red Bull KTM Ajo) tagged Celestino Vietti’s (BETA Tools SpeedRS Team) Boscoscuro and crashed at the opening corner from the top six. Meanwhile, Gonzalez was demoted to P4 by a hard-charging Daniel Muñoz (Italtrans Racing Team), with the latter soon slotting himself into P2 behind leader Escrig after carving past Holgado on Lap 2. On Guevara watch, the rider second in the title race made a promising getaway from 10 th on the grid. The #28 was up to P7, as David Alonso (CFMOTO Power Electronics Aspar Team) then shoved Gonzalez back to P5 at the start of Lap 3. And talking of being shoved back, Guevara lost a spot to Ortola at the beginning of Lap 4 – the title contender was now P8. On Lap 8, Ortola then sailed past Gonzalez for P4, with Guevara now behind Gonzalez’s teammate Senna Agius in P9. Both of the title chasers were going the wrong way in Qatar, while the Aspar duo of Alonso and Holgado began to reel in Escrig. 0.5s split the trio at the halfway point, before it became a quartet as Ortola dragged himself into the podium places, with Alonso the one slipping back to P4 – and Holgado shadowing Escrig. Then, a couple of laps later on Lap 14, huge title race drama unravelled. Guevara was cruising. There was a problem with the Spaniard’s bike going into Turn 1 and for the first time in 13 months, Guevara was out of a Grand Prix. Cruel in the extreme. Up front, Holgado stole P1 from Escrig and immediately put 1.2s, then 1.6s, into Escrig. And in terms of the title fight, Muñoz re-passed Gonzalez to see the latter drop to P6, but at this stage, it was all about bringing his Triumph-Kalex to the finish. The late race pace from Holgado was unrivalled. After finishing P2 last weekend in Malaysia, the #96 went one better in Qatar to notch up his second win of the season, while Ortola dished out some late heartache to Escrig to win the photo-finish run to the line after getting a brilliant launch out of the final corner to grab P2. In the end, Alonso finished 1.8s away from the Ortola-Escrig scrap in P4, as Muñoz rounded out the top five. Then came a frustrated Gonzalez in P6, but once the dust settles, the #18 will realise he’s now 13.5 points clear of Guevara, meaning outscoring his rival in Portugal by 12 points next time out will see him clinch the 2026 crown. Agius was 0.6s away from his teammate in P7, as Jose Antonio Rueda (Red Bull KTM Ajo) earned an equal-best Moto2 finish in P8. Closing out the top 10 were Filip Salač (OnlyFans American Racing Team) and Vietti, the latter unable to fight his way back through the pack after the early contact with Veijer. And so, onto Portimao we go, with the title-chase momentum swinging right into the hands of Gonzalez. The Season Finale is now streaming, don’t miss anything with MotoGP™ VideoPass

signals.title: Bezzecchi bounces back with Qatar victory as Marquez extends championship lead
signals.summary: The Italian keeps his faint title hopes alive with a dominant win under the Lusail lights as the #93 strides to P2 ahead of Fernandez, with Martin digging deep for P7 The championship chase rolls on to the Portuguese Grand Prix. Under the lights in Lusail, Marco Bezzecchi (Aprilia Racing) bounced back from Saturday's low to rise highest on Sunday, keeping himself in the title race frame. That's the Italian's 12th MotoGP win and his most important to date, but it's second-place finisher Marc Marquez (Ducati Lenovo Team) who takes another step towards retaining his crown after collecting 20 points at the Qatar Airways Grand Prix of Qatar. Third went the way of Raul Fernandez (SuperFile Trackhouse MotoGP Team), who returns to action in classy fashion while still nursing two broken fingers. That's the #25's sixth Sunday rostrum of the campaign, and speaking of injured heroes, Jorge Martin (Aprilia Racing) comes across the line in P7 just two weeks after breaking his wrist to remain in the championship hunt. Superhuman. The potential title-decider got underway with polesitter Bezzecchi closing the door and keeping the lead going into Turn 1 ahead of Marc Marquez, before Fernandez dived past the World Championship leader to demote the #93 to P3. Martin got a decent start – the #89 was briefly up to P8 from P11 on the grid before a slow-starting Fabio Di Giannantonio (Pertamina Enduro VR46 Racing Team) barged his way through on the rider second in the title race at Turn 12 on the opening lap. By Lap 3, Bezzecchi and Fernandez were over 1.5s up the road from Marc Marquez, who had 2027 teammate Pedro Acosta (Red Bull KTM Factory Racing) climbing all over the rear wheel of the Ducati. Until he wasn’t. Acosta passed Marquez at Turn 15 on Lap 3 to jump into the final podium spot, and a little earlier in the lap, Martin climbed up to P8 after a good move was made on Johann Zarco (Castrol Honda LCR). On the sixth lap, Acosta looked like he allowed Marquez to come back through at Turn 2. The obvious answer was Acosta receiving tyre pressure warnings on his dashboard, as the #37 slotted in behind the seven-time MotoGP World Champion. It promoted Marquez back up to P3, three seconds away from second-place Fernandez, with Martin still lapping in P8. At the halfway stage of the Grand Prix, Bezzecchi led Fernandez by 1.2s, with Marquez and Acosta still locked together, 3.9s off the lead. Enea Bastianini (Red Bull KTM Tech3) and Ai Ogura (SuperFile Trackhouse MotoGP Team) were squabbling away in P5 and P6, just over a second away from the Ducati and KTM stars, with Martin climbing to P7 on Lap 11 as Di Giannantonio struggled with pace. On Lap 14, Marc Marquez began to turn up the wick. A fastest lap of the Grand Prix was slammed in, a 1:52.558, which was nearly eight tenths quicker than Bezzecchi, and nearly nine tenths faster than Fernandez. Acosta was now 1.2s away from Marquez and chasing the #37 was now Ogura after the Japanese rider barged through on Bastianini on Lap 15 of 22. Bezzecchi and Fernandez stepped their pace back up over the next couple of laps to stabilise the gap to Marquez, but it did then dip below a second for the first time on Lap 17 between Fernandez and Marquez. Every point matters in the title chase, and with Martin digging deep and through the pain barrier in P7, it was vital for the #89 that Fernandez kept Marquez at bay. But it was looking increasingly unlikely. With four laps to go, Marquez had a real sniff of P2. Then, in one of the easiest passes Marquez will have had in a long time, the championship leader grabbed P2 from Fernandez on the run out of the final corner to provisionally pocket an extra four crucial points. One lap remaining then. Bezzecchi led onto it by 3.6s to keep his slim title hopes alive, with Marquez holding Fernandez behind him by 0.5s. Ogura was closing in on the podium fight, but it was too little too late for the Dutch GP winner. Fair play to Bezzecchi. After a crushing Tissot Sprint crash on Saturday, the Italian led from start to finish to collect 25 points in Doha and make sure the championship chase rolls into Portimao in a couple of weeks. It was the #93 who collected 20 points to take another step towards an eighth MotoGP title, with the points lead sitting at 60 with 74 remaining. Fernandez clung on, but it wasn’t quite enough for the rider still nursing two broken right fingers to clinch P2. Still, a podium with those injuries signals a top job done by the British GP winner. Ogura crossed the line just 1.2s away from his teammate in P4, with Bastianini fronting the KTM charge in P5 ahead of a frustrated Acosta who on more than one occasion looked like he was having tyre pressure issues. It was P6 at the flag for the #37. Coming home in P7 was Martin. A Sprint podium and nine more points on Sunday is a superhero effort from the 2024 World Champion, just two weeks on from breaking his wrist in Australia. It’s valuable points lost in the title race of course, but scoring solid points this weekend is a win in itself for Martin. And, importantly, the #89 is still in title contention. Di Giannantonio struggled unexpectedly to finish P8 from the front row, while Zarco and Iker Lecuona, Alex Marquez’s BK8 Gresini Racing MotoGP stand-in, completed the top 10. Four more finishers pocketed points in the form of Franco Morbidelli (Pertamina Enduro VR46 Racing Team), Fermin Aldeguer (BK8 Gresini Racing MotoGP), Maverick Viñales (Red Bull KTM Tech3), and Joan Mir’s stand-in, Jake Dixon (Honda HRC Castrol). The Briton scoring points for the first time in MotoGP in P14, with Diogo Moreira (Pro Honda LCR) and Brad Binder (Red Bull KTM Factory Racing) forced to retire from the Grand Prix with problems. So we head to the Portuguese Grand Prix, with three riders still in contention for the 2026 title, but the Aprilias of Martin and Bezzecchi have several mountains to climb at the rollercoaster. 60 points in it between our two most recent World Champions in Marquez

signals.title: Quiles makes quick work of Qatar Qualifying
signals.summary: The World Champion takes a sixth career pole ahead of Almansa and Uriarte in a mis-timed last lap rush Maximo Quiles (CFMOTO Gaviota Aspar Team) made it back-to-back Moto3 poles at the Qatar Airways Grand Prix of Qatar, but the real drama came as the clock ticked down in a truly bizarre end to Q2. The World Champion's 2:02.288 proved untouchable, with David Almansa (Liqui Moly Dynavolt Intact GP) just 0.155s adrift and Brian Uriarte (Red Bull KTM Ajo) completing the front row after a frantic final flying lap. Who’s got the pace for pole? The lightweight class goes all out for the top spot on the grid at Lusail. The #28 wasted little time stamping his authority on qualifying, setting his pole-worthy lap on just his third lap of Lusail. Almansa was his closest challenger, with Alvaro Carpe (Red Bull KTM Ajo), Uriarte and David Muñoz (Liqui Moly Dynavolt Intact GP) completing the provisional top five as riders headed into the pits with six minutes remaining. Then came a game of waiting. And waiting. And waiting... Fresh tyres fitted, clock ticking, and a high-stakes game of chicken unfolded in pit lane. Nobody wanted to blink first, but with every second wasted, the chance of one final flyer was slipping away. Hakim Danish (AEON Credit – MT Helmets – MSI) finally broke the deadlock, with Quiles and Almansa feigning their exits before eventually heading out with just 2:10 remaining. With lap times around the 2:02 mark, had they left it late to cross the line and start their final flyers? A huge group of riders arrived at Turn 16 almost side by side, all scrambling to make the line in time. Most succeeded, but Quiles, Almansa and Carpe had left it too late. The chequered flag was already out, and their final opportunities had vanished before they could even begin. For Quiles, his early benchmark was already looking good enough. Almansa, however, had thrown away a golden chance to attack pole, with Liqui Moly Dynavolt Intact GP Team Principal Peter Öttl explaining that the #22 had wanted to head out alone. Instead, he didn't get a final flying lap at all. Carpe came off worst in the late-session gamble, losing his front-row spot as Uriarte stormed to third. Danish briefly jumped to fourth before being shuffled back to seventh, while Muñoz and Fernandez climbed to fifth and sixth, leaving Carpe heading row two after a costly miscalculation. Quiles on pole, Almansa alongside him, Uriarte looking to strike from third and Carpe with a point to prove from fourth. The Championship's leading quartet are perfectly poised for a Lusail showdown on Sunday! The Season Finale is now streaming, don’t miss anything with MotoGP™ VideoPass

signals.title: Match point Sunday: Marquez wins dramatic Qatar Sprint, Martin heroic for P3, Bezzecchi crashes
signals.summary: You couldn't squeeze much more drama into a Tissot Sprint evening as the red corner takes another step towards the crown A drama-drenched Tissot Sprint, anyone? Well, that's exactly what was served up at the Qatar Airways Grand Prix of Qatar. So many storylines. The chief among them was Marc Marquez (Ducati Lenovo Team), the Doha Sprint gold medallist, earning 12 points to head into Sunday's Grand Prix with a championship match point. The rider with the biggest chance of stopping the #93 from clinching a famous eighth MotoGP title is the heroic Jorge Martin (Aprilia Racing) after the #89's teammate, Marco Bezzecchi, crashed out after contact with Marquez, to see the Italian face a mammoth mountain to climb if he's to win the 2026 title. From P11 on the grid, Martin rolled out a stunner just two weeks on from breaking his right wrist to finish in an unbelievable P3, with Fabio Di Giannantonio (Pertamina Enduro VR46 Racing Team) passing the 2024 World Champion on the final lap to see the Italian earn Saturday silver. All of this means it's 49 points between Marquez and Martin heading into Sunday's highly anticipated Grand Prix, while Bezzecchi sits 79 adrift. It was a lightning launch away from the lights from polesitter Bezzecchi, who just about held off the challenge of Marquez from the middle of the front row. Francesco Bagnaia briefly demoted his Ducati Lenovo teammate to second at Turn 2, before the #93 got the cutback on the exit and held position. Martin, meanwhile, didn’t make up any places for the majority of the first lap from his P11 starting slot, as we then saw Fermin Aldeguer (BK8 Gresini Racing MotoGP) wipe out Bagnaia at the final corner on Lap 1. Aldeguer, lunging up the inside of Pedro Acosta (Red Bull KTM Factory Racing), got it wrong at Turn 16. The Spaniard was far too late on the brakes, and in the wrong place at the wrong time was Pecco. The Italian was collected by Aldeguer, which sent the double MotoGP champion flying from his Ducati Desmosedici. The red flags were waved while Pecco was being stretchered away from the gravel trap, with the #63 thankfully conscious and talking before he was taken to the medical centre. The incident saw Aldeguer receive a double Long Lap penalty for the restarted Sprint. After a brief pause, a 10-lap Sprint burst back into life. And this time around, Marquez got the jump and collected the holeshot ahead of Bezzecchi and Di Giannantonio. Martin was out of the blocks better, the rider second in the standings was up to P6 on the opening lap, and then Martin carved past Raul Fernandez (SuperFiles Trackhouse MotoGP Team) for P5. Top work from the wounded 2024 MotoGP World Champion. It was then P4. And just up the road, Bezzecchi challenged Marquez at Turn 15 on Lap 2, but it didn’t work. The red corner bit back brilliantly to hold onto P1. Then, more drama. Bezzecchi saw a small gap open with Marquez slightly wide, and when the #93 came back on-line to grab a late apex, the duo came into contact. Marquez defending; Bezzecchi seizing an opportunity, the latter then crashing. Bezzecchi was out of the Sprint in dramatic fashion, and that was a potential championship chase ending DNF for the Italian. The Stewards had a look and decided that no further action was needed. A racing incident. Then, suddenly, Martin was attacking Marquez. This was a superhuman effort from the rider who broke their wrist two weeks ago in Australia. It was a pass that ultimately didn’t work and then over the next few laps, the championship leader grew his lead out to 0.8s with three to go, as Martin then had to enter defensive mode with Di Giannantonio climbing all over his rear wheel. So much so, the Italian made his move on the final lap at Turn 2. This was significant, because a gold medal for Marquez and a bronze for Martin would mean a title chance is coming on Sunday. What a Sprint. Drama from start to finish. A record 25 th Sprint win goes to Marc Marquez and the situation is now like this: if Marquez wins the Grand Prix and Martin doesn’t score a point on Sunday, an eighth MotoGP title would land in the lap of the 33-year-old. Di Giannantonio’s last-lap pass hands the Italian a silver, and Marquez his chance tomorrow, as Martin delivers a simply unbelievable performance. Heroic. From P11 on the grid, with a fractured right wrist, the #89 couldn’t have done anything else, as full focus now turns to Sunday's main event. Bezzecchi’s DNF doesn't mean the #72 is mathematically out of contention for the 2026 crown just yet, but it's another almighty blow to the fading chances. The fallout? To be seen and heard ahead of tomorrow’s Grand Prix. It was Fernandez who clinched P4 ahead of the impressive Johann Zarco (Castrol Honda LCR), with Acosta just shading Ai Ogura (SuperFile Trackhouse MotoGP Team) across the line to see the KTM and Trackhouse stars collect P6 and P7. P8 went to Enea Bastianini (Red Bull KTM Tech3), while the final point was gathered up by Alex Marquez’s BK8 Gresini Racing MotoGP stand-in, Iker Lecuona. That’s a top job done by the 2026 WorldSBK runner-up. It’s a long shot, but there’s a chance. High drama. High controversy. And a highly motivated Marc Marquez hunting a crown that a few months ago was well out of reach. Can Aprilia and Martin ensure the title scrap goes to Portugal? And how will Bezzecchi bounce back from Saturday’s disappointment? We’ll find out at 19:00 local time in Doha. The Season Finale is now streaming, don’t miss anything with MotoGP™ VideoPass

signals.title: Escrig untouchable as Gonzalez wins battle of wits with Guevara
signals.summary: The KLINT Racing Team rider dominates Qatar qualifying, but a clever late move from Gonzalez steals the spotlight in the Championship fight Alex Escrig (KLINT Racing Team) was in a league of his own in Qatar, storming to a maiden Moto2 pole with a record-breaking 1:55.241. But behind him, Manuel Gonzalez (LIQUI MOLY Dynavolt Intact GP) pulled off a masterstroke to snatch second, while title rival Izan Guevara (BLU CRU Pramac Yamaha Moto2) was left languishing in seventh, with just 3.5 points separating the pair in the Championship. That was the case before several grid penalties were handed out late in the day, including for Gonzalez and Guevara. The reason? Slow on line coming out of the pit lane and impeding Daniel Muñoz's (Italtrans Racing Team) lap, which means the starting slots for the top two for Sunday's Grand Prix are as follows: P5 for Gonzalez, and P10 for Guevara. The fight for pole is on! Who will come out on top as the intermediate class sets the grid for Sunday’s race? Escrig laid down the gauntlet with a stunning 1:55.241, ahead of Guevara and Daniel Holgado (CFMOTO Power Electronics Aspar Team), while Gonzalez languished in ninth when, with seven minutes remaining, the field went into pit lane before a frantic final shootout. Celestino Vietti (BETA Tools SpeedRS Team) then snatched provisional second, while Escrig came within just 0.009s of improving his own record. But all eyes were turning to Gonzalez who was tucked in behind Guevara looking to profit from a valuable tow. The Championship leaders got stuck in traffic behind Xabi Zurutuza (KLINT Racing Team), Gonzalez made his first move at Turn 16, sweeping past Guevara. Crossing the line seventh but that wasn't good enough. One final flyer. One last chance. Gonzalez dived past Zurutuza and into clear air, leaving Guevara trapped behind the KLINT Racing rider. The Championship leader then fired in barnstorming 1:55.367 to snatch second, while his title rival could only watch his front-row hopes disappear, settling for seventh. Holgado secured third, just 0.233s off pole, with Vietti pushed back to fourth. Collin Veijer (Red Bull KTM Ajo) took fifth ahead of Senna Agius (LIQUI MOLY Dynavolt Intact GP), while Guevara was meant to lead row three alongside Jose Antonio Rueda (Red Bull KTM Ajo) and Adrian Huertas (Italtrans Racing Team). Others with penalties include Agius, Huertas, Barry Baltus (REDS Fantic Racing), Zonta van den Goorbergh, the Dutchman's Momoven Idrofoglia RW Racing teammate Ayumu Sasaki, and Zurutuza. That means the front row consists of Escrig, Holgado and Vietti; the second row is Veijer, Gonzalez and Rueda, with Guevara fronting the fourth row. So, Escrig celebrates a maiden pole and new Lusail lap record, becoming 2026’s 12th different Moto2 polesitter. But the focus will be on Gonzalez and Guevara, with just 3.5 points separating them going into Sunday in Doha. The Season Finale is now streaming, don’t miss anything with MotoGP™ VideoPass

signals.title: Bezzecchi smashes lap record to deny Marquez, Martin P11
signals.summary: The #72 takes pole as he makes a final stand – with Marquez second and Diggia locking out the front row at Lusail Marco Bezzecchi (Aprilia Racing) took a lap record pole position for the Qatar Airways Grand Prix of Qatar, setting a new 1:50.028 to pull clear of Marc Marquez (Ducati Lenovo Team) by more than a quarter of a second. Marquez lines up second as he looks to set up a championship point for Sunday, with Fabio Di Giannantonio (Pertamina Enduro VR46 Racing Team) completing the front row. Bezzecchi will be aiming to make his own final stand and cut his 67-point deficit this weekend, but to have a Championship point on Sunday, it’s Jorge Martin (Aprilia Racing) that Marc Marquez needs to outscore in the Tissot Sprint – by five points. The #89 starts down in P11 after a messier qualifying session – but not one where he was lacking outright speed. Can he make a comeback? Q1 First, Q1. Pedro Acosta (Red Bull KTM Factory) was leading the way with a comfortable margin as they headed out for their second runs, with the #37 a rare sight in the Q1 session and looking to ease through. Fermin Aldeguer (BK8 Gresini Racing MotoGP) found something in the locker round his next lap though, taking over on top with two minutes left on the clock. The final train round saw Acosta leading a quartet of riders all looking to improve, and the #37 did but it wasn’t enough to topple Aldeguer from the top. Still, Acosta headed through alongside the #54. Q2 Much was on the line for Aprilia – and the 2026 championship fight – as the field rolled out of pitlane to begin Q2. Marc Marquez set the a serious benchmark on the first runs, but that didn’t last too long as a stunning lap came in from a key rival: Bezzecchi. The #72 smashed the all-time lap record with a 1:50.065, taking the honours from Friday’s fastest, Fabio Di Giannantonio (Pertamina Enduro VR46 Racing Team). That left Bez at the top, 0.296 ahead of Marc Marquez, with Raul Fernandez (SuperFile Trackhouse MotoGP Team) in a provisional P3. With three minutes left on the clock, everyone was back out and Marquez was beginning another fast one. Up through sector 1 by eight hundredths, up through sector 2 by eight hundredths, losing out in sector 3 and then crossing the line two tenths off, that was that for the points leader – no pole, provisional second place, and waiting for the rest to put their final laps in. For Bezzecchi, it was another lap record. The #72 took a further 0.037 off his best to head Marquez by 0.266, with all eyes on Martin as he looked to improve from P11. It wasn’t to be however, as the #89 encountered Acosta a bit closer than he would have liked round the final sector and couldn’t improve – sitting up angrily as he was left in P11 on the grid. THE GRID Up top it’s Bezzecchi, who needs to make big gains to get a foot back in the title fight. Marquez lines up second as he looks to outscore Martin by 30 points and Bezzecchi by eight points this weekend to take the Championship. 2023 Qatar GP winner Diggia, after topping the timesheets on Friday, lines up third. Fernandez is forced to settle for fourth after a big moment for him ruining his last lap, with Francesco Bagnaia (Ducati Lenovo Team) up in fifth. Ai Ogura (SuperFile Trackhouse MotoGP Team) takes P6, completing Row 2. Johann Zarco (Castrol Honda LCR) is next up as he heads Row 3 from Acosta and Aldeguer, with the Q1 graduates in reverse order on that third row. Enea Bastianini (Red Bull KTM Tech3) completes the top ten as Martin faces down a rescue mission from P11, ahead of only Brad Binder (Red Bull KTM Factory Racing) after the South African crashed early in the session, rider ok. The grids are set, the championship fight is hotting up in the desert – and the Tissot Sprint will decide if Marc Marquez has a match point on Sunday. Tune in for that as we go racing under the floodlights in Lusail! The Season Finale is now streaming, don’t miss anything with MotoGP™ VideoPass

signals.title: Bagnaia out of Qatar GP with right foot fractures
signals.summary: The double World Champion will be absent from the grid on Sunday following his fall in the Sprint Get well soon, Pecco! After what was a promising weekend, Francesco Bagnaia ’s (Ducati Lenovo Team) Qatar GP has come to a premature end after a Lap 1 fall following a collision with Fermin Aldeguer (BK8 Gresini Racing MotoGP). Pecco was the innocent party after Aldeguer hit the back of his Ducati into Turn 16, flicking the #63 into the air. The red flag was brought out as the Italian was stretchered away and following examination, has since been diagnosed with two fractures in his foot, ruling him out of action for Sunday. Angel Charte, MotoGP Medical Director, provided an update on the #63’s condition: “Initial medical examinations carried out on Francesco Bagnaia at the Lusail International Circuit Medical Centre have revealed two fractures in his right foot, involving the fourth and fifth metatarsals. The rider will be transferred to Doha Hospital tonight for further tests to determine whether the fractures require surgery.” The Season Finale is now streaming, don’t miss anything with MotoGP™ VideoPass

signals.title: Marc Marquez fastest from Bezzecchi, Martin P5 in Qatar FP1

It wasn’t the end of the session the rider fourth in the standings would have wanted, though, because a late issue with his RC16 ended FP1 prematurely for Acosta, who is still mathematically in contention for the title. signals.title: Quiles heads Almansa in Moto3 Practice, Carpe and Uriarte in Q1 in Qatar

signals.title: Di Giannantonio P1 under the lights at Lusail, Marquez and Martin in Q2
signals.summary: The Italian set a new lap record for Practice honours whilst the top two in the Championship will be going head-to-head on Saturday Putting on a show under the lights, Fabio Di Giannantonio (Pertamina Enduro VR46 Racing Team) was untouchable on Friday evening to bag P1 in Practice and to lead the field into Sprint Saturday. The Italian set a new lap record with a 1’50.406 seeing him with nearly a tenth and a half over nearest rival Marc Marquez (Ducati Lenovo Team) who suffered a chain failure whilst Marco Bezzecchi (Aprilia Racing) leads the Noale brand’s charge in third. Straight down to business and competitive from the first lap, ‘Bez’ placed himself up at the front and improved straight away on his second run too – and he wasn’t the only Aprilia in good form. Returning to action after sitting out most of the Malaysian GP, 2024 World Champion Jorge Martin (Aprilia Racing) was up in the top ten, aiming to book a spot straight into Q2. Ai Ogura (SuperFile Trackhouse MotoGP Team) and teammate Raul Fernandez were also making it a great day for the Noale factory, both up inside the provisional Q2 places. Climbing the order having led at the very start of the session, Di Giannantonio took over at the top with a 1’51.174, more than 1.5s quicker than he went in FP1. Marquez and teammate Francesco Bagnaia (Ducati Lenovo Team) were fifth and sixth but the #93 suffered a setback when the chain sprung off his GP26 Desmosedici with a little under 30 minutes on the clock. Far from ideal as he trundled down pitlane, an unexpected pause into the reigning World Champion’s second run. The delay wasn’t too long for Marquez as he hit the track with 18 minutes left on the clock. With just under a quarter of an hour remaining, the #93 got himself back into P1 with the first 1’50 of the weekend – a 1’50.925, undeterred by his previous disruption. signals.title: More races, more tracks: 2027 Bagger World Cup calendar announced
signals.summary: The second season of the FIM Harley-Davidson Bagger World Cup sees the series expand as the new calendar – and next gen bike – are revealed at EICMA Harley-Davidson has unveiled key developments for the second season of the FIM Harley-Davidson Bagger World Cup Tuned by Dynojet. An expanded calendar has been revealed, with eight rounds and 16 races across seven countries, including three new MotoGP™ venues. Five teams and 11 motorcycles have been confirmed for 2027, and there is development coming to the machinery too – with increased performance, improved handling and new aerodynamic bodywork under development. Following a successful inaugural season, the championship enters its second year with a broader international calendar, an upgraded race motorcycle and new opportunities for fans and teams. The inaugural championship produced five different race winners, podium finishes for every team and a title fight involving four riders heading into the final round. Archie McDonald (Joe Rascal Racing) secured the inaugural Bagger World Cup title in Austria. The expanded calendar builds on the enthusiastic reception the Bagger World Cup received from MotoGP spectators and Harley-Davidson fans during its inaugural season, bringing the series to new audiences while strengthening its presence at established events. The season will once again open at the MotoGP Grand Prix of the United States, at the Circuit of The Americas in Austin, Texas, on April 23–25, following an official preseason test April 17–18. Three new destinations join the calendar: MotoGP Grand Prix of France: Le Mans brings the Bagger World Cup to one of MotoGP's largest and most passionate audiences. MotoGP Grand Prix of Portugal: Portimão will host the season finale, where the second Bagger World Cup Champion will be crowned, extending the racing season from April through October. signals.title: Statt großer Aufregung – Zufriedenheit in Katar bei KTM-Pilot Acosta (6.)
signals.summary: Zu Beginn des Wüsten-GP in Katar zog KTM-Frontmann sogar Pedro Acosta an WM-Favorit Marc Marquez vorbei. Im Finish wurde es nur Platz 6. Diesmal kein Grund, sich aufzuregen, Acosta zog zufrieden ab. Dass KTM-Werksfahrer Pedro Acosta beim Wüsten-GP in Katar nach der Zielankunft auf Platz 6 nicht auszuckte, wird bei einem Blick auf die Freitags-Statistik verständlich. Der junge Spanier war im Zeittraining erstmals in der Saison 2026 am direkten Q2-Einzug gescheitert. Es fehlte auf dem haftfreudigen Losail-Circuit schlicht der Speed, um konstant an der Spitze mitzufahren. Dazu kamen technische Probleme, die Acosta zweimal von der Arbeit abhielten. Im Sprintrennen war die Nummer 37 wie die meisten Piloten mit den Medium-Reifen gestartet. Der Schachzug reichte am Samstag für Endrang 6 – und Acosta konnte sich als bester KTM-Athlet behaupten. Beim Großen Preis von Katar gelang das, bei durchaus vergleichbarem Rennverlauf, nicht. In Runde 18 musste sich Acosta Tech3-Pilot Enea Bastianini geschlagen geben. Eine halbe Sekunde hinter dem Italiener und zehn Sekunden hinter dem siegreichen Bezzecchi ging es über die Linie. Dabei sah es nach erneut starkem Start zunächst bestens für die offizielle Werksmannschaft aus. Acosta biss sich am berechnend fahrenden Marc Marquez fest und zog im dritten Umlauf vorbei. Doch der Traum vom Podest erfüllte sich in der Hitze von Katar nicht. Acosta bestätigte nach dem Rennen Probleme mit dem Reifenluftdruck, verwies aber auf ein anderes Problem: «Ja, der Luftdruck war ein Thema, aber wir hatten am Bike ein anderes Problem, das diese Geschichte noch verschlimmert hat. Es war ein Problem, das erstmals im GP aufgetaucht ist. Wir müssen erst noch verstehen, was es war und warum ich langsamer wurde.» Fakt ist: Eine Strafe wegen Unterschreitung des Mindestluftdrucks blieb nach dem GP aus. Sogleich fügte Acosta dazu: «Aber ich hatte so oder so nicht das Tempo, um mit Marc zu kämpfen. Die Fahrt auf Platz 4 wäre normal möglich gewesen, eventuell sogar ein Kampf um das Podest – aber Marc musste ich ziehen lassen. Am Anfang ist er zurückhaltend gefahren, wollte das Rennen nicht am Anfang entscheiden, aber später hat er nachgelegt. Ehrlich – ich bin nicht unzufrieden mit dem, wie die Rennen geendet haben. Ich bin sogar happy, denn wir haben hier die richtigen Entscheidungen getroffen. Es war ein Risiko, aber wir haben es geschafft, das Wochenende zu drehen.» Waren es vielleicht die Bedingungen, die Acosta einbremsten? Auch hier wiegelte der WM-Vierte ruhig und kompakt ab: «Nein, ich kann nicht sagen, dass sich die Strecke großartig verändert hat, auch der Wind ging in Ordnung.» Wenig erbaulich war der Blick für Acosta auf die WM-Tabelle. Trotz zweimal 10 Punkten für die sechsten Ränge zog der WM-Dritte Bezzecchi weiter von Acosta davon und von hinten rückte Ai Ogura näher (minus 15 Punkte). Mit 48 Punkten Rückstand auf Bezzecchi ist die Chance, die KTM-Ära mit Platz 3 abzuschließen, nur minimal. Der WM-Zug war bereits nach dem Sprint am Samstag abgefahren. Souveräner Sieg! signals.title: MotoGP-Held 2.0 Jorge Martin mit Ansage: «Will dieses Jahr noch gewinnen»
signals.summary: Aprilia-Werksfahrer Jorge Martin gelang das, was noch vor wenigen Tagen unmöglich schien. Der «Martinator» holte in beiden Katar-Rennen Punkte und half aktiv mit die WM-Titelentscheidung zu vertagen. Jorge Martin leistete beim Katar-GP, zwei Wochen nach seinem Highspeed-Crash auf Phillip Island, mit gebrochenem Handgelenk Unfassbares. Am Freitag gelang der direkte Einzug ins zweite Qualifying, im Q2 holte sich Martin Platz 11, um im Sprint durchs Feld zu schmettern. Die Zuschauer rieben sich verwundert die Augen – Martin führte den Sprint vor Marc Marquez an. Am Ende wurde es Platz 3. Beim Großen Preis über die doppelte Distanz ging der Madrilene ebenfalls nicht in die Knie. Von Startplatz 10 kämpfte sich die Nummer 89 an Johann Zarco und im späteren Verlauf an den Platz 3 losgefahrenen Fabio Di Giannantonio vorbei. Eine weitere Position gewann Martin durch die Long-Lap von Fermin Aldeguer. Den Zielstrich erreichte der völlig verausgabte WM-Zweite 14 Sekunden hinter dem Rennsieger aus dem eigenen Rennstall. Auf die schnellste Rennrunde, die an Marc Marquez ging, verlor der angeschlagene Spanier 0,5 Sekunden. Der Champion von 2024, der vor einem Jahr bei seinem Katar-Debüt mit der RS-GP schwer gestürzt war, schaffte es dennoch zum Austausch mit den Medien. Martins Bericht: «Jetzt bin ich komplett erledigt, aber es war es wert, alles zu geben, auch wenn ich jetzt recht starke Schmerzen habe. Aber mir bleiben jetzt zwei Wochen, in denen ich mich erholen und auch die Heilung des Bruchs voranreiben kann. Ich gehe davon aus, dass ich in Portimao nahe bei 100 Prozent sein kann.» Der kämpferische Spanier weiter: «Wir sind hierhergekommen, haben alles gegeben und unser Ziel erreicht. Es freut mich für das ganze Team, es tut allen gut, so einen Erfolg zu erleben. Wenn ich bedenke, dass ich letzten Dienstag nicht einmal wusste, ob ich hier sein kann – und am Samstag auf dem Podest stand, das ist schon sehr speziell.» Martin über den Verlauf des GP-Rennens: «Leider war die Ausgangslage mit Startplatz 11 und 10 nicht sehr gut. Ich hatte aber das Tempo, um mich im Bereich von Platz 5 zu bewegen, mehr ging nicht. Es hat mich sehr gefreut, auch wieder von «Diggia» zu fahren und das Resultat zu sichern – wobei ich in den letzten Runden komplett zerstört war.» Und Martins Blick auf die nächste Runde in Portugal? «Mir ist es wichtig, dass ich meine Zeit bei Aprilia für mich und das ganze Team mit Erfolg beende. Mein Ziel ist, dieses Jahr noch zu gewinnen. Ich hoffe, dass mein Körper es zulässt, wieder an der Spitze zu kämpfen und alles für die WM zu tun. In Malaysia konnte ich eigentlich gar nichts unternehmen, hier aber bereits unser Ziel geschafft, also kämpfen wir in Portimao wie bisher», so die Ansage des «Martinators». Die Ausgangslage vor Runde 21: Marc Marquez mit 431 hat 60 Zählern Vorsprung auf Jorge Martin. Damit fehlen dem Ducati nur noch 12 Punkte, bereits im Sprint kann die Titelfrage mit einem Sieg von «MM93» geklärt sein. Gewinnt Martin, bleibt die WM weiter offen. Die Zeit spielt für Martin – der WM-Herausforderer hat nun 12 Tage, um sich von seinen Heldenfahrten in der Wüste zu erholen – und die nächsten Attacken vorzubereiten. Souveräner Sieg! signals.title: Trackhouse-Ass Ai Ogura (4.) hatte viele Zweikämpfe: «Ich bin nicht happy!»
signals.summary: Im MotoGP-Grand-Prix in Katar duellierte sich Ai Ogura (Aprilia) mit Johann Zarco, Enea Bastianini und Pedro Acosta. Viele Überholmanöver prägten sein Rennen – er war alles andere als zufrieden. Ai Ogura startete am Sonntag von Position 5 in das MotoGP-Rennen in Katar. In der ersten Runde konnte der Trackhouse-Aprilia-Pilot eine Position gut machen, nachdem Fabio Di Giannantonio (VR46 Ducati) einen miserablen Start erwischt hatte. Auf Position 4 liegend musste er sich aber vehement gegen LCR-Honda-Pilot Johann Zarco verteidigen. In Runde 3 fielen die beiden auch noch hinter das KTM-Duo Pedro Acosta und Enea Bastianini zurück. Danach steckte Ogura viele Runden lang hinter Bastianini auf Platz 6 fest. Mehrere Versuche, den Italiener zu überholen, scheiterten. Doch im 15. Umlauf konnte sich der Japaner am Tech3-Fahrer vorbeiquetschen. In Runde 17 schnappte sich Ogura auch noch Acosta – der Spanier hatte allerdings mit einem zu niedrigen Druck im Vorderreifen zu kämpfen, weshalb er sich während des Rennens mehrere Male zurückfallen ließ. Im Finish machte Ogura Jagd auf Marc Marquez (Ducati) und Trackhouse-Teamkollege Raul Fernandez, doch es war zu spät. Der Moto2-Weltmeister von 2024 überquerte die Ziellinie mit 4,885 sec Rückstand auf Sieger Marco Bezzecchi (Aprilia). Ist Ogura mit seinem Rennen zufrieden? «Nein. Ich bin nicht happy», schmunzelte der 25-Jährige. «Im ersten Teil habe ich zu viel mit Johann gekämpft. Ich war nicht schnell genug und er dachte sich, dass wenn er mich nicht überholt, er viel Zeit verlieren würde. Also versuchte er, mich zu überholen. Wir beide hatten einen unterschiedlichen Ansatz, deshalb haben wir sehr gekämpft. Das war keine ideale Situation.» Mit seinem Speed am Ende des Rennens war Ogura dennoch zufrieden. «Gegen Ende war meine Pace ganz okay. Ich habe den Reifen gut verwaltet», erklärte er. «Es gibt ein paar positive Dinge aber mehr negative.» Ai Ogura belegte in Katar die Ränge 7 und 4. In der WM-Tabelle ist er vor den letzten beiden Saisonevents mit 294 Punkten auf Position 5 zu finden. Souveräner Sieg! signals.title: Enea Bastianini (KTM/5.): Blitz-Start im Katar-GP– dann starkes Chattering
signals.summary: Red Bull Tech3-Fahrer Enea Bastianini nutzte die Gunst der Stunde, kürte sich beim MotoGP-Rennen in der Wüste von Katar zum besten KTM-Piloten und sprach dann über ein geplantes Geschenk an das Team. Enea Bastianini produzierte auf dem Lusail International Circuit von Doha bei Flutlicht am Sonntag von Position 9 einen ausgezeichneten Start. Bereits in Runde 2 wurde der Italiener an fünfter Position geführt. Am Ende gelang Platz 5 ins Ziel zu bringen. Der 28-Jährige fuhr mit der Red Bull Tech3-KTM lange hinter seinem Markenkollegen Pedro Acosta, der jedoch verzweifelt auf der Suche nach Windschatten war, um seinen Reifendruck im Vorderrad steigen zu lassen. So kam «La Bestia» vier Runden vor Schluss auch noch am Spanier vorbei. «Es war ein hartes Rennen», erklärte Bastianini, der im kommenden Jahr auf der Trackhouse-Aprilia sitzen wird und dem 6,9 Sekunden auf Sieger Marco Bezzecchi fehlten. «Mein Start war gut, ich hatte eine gute Linie und war in Kurve 1 in einer guten Position. Ich wollte dranbleiben und mit Pedro und Marc um das Podium kämpfen, aber in der mittleren Phase des Rennens hat Marc dann ausgecheckt.» Der Italiener von der Adria berichtete weiter: «Ich hatte das ganze Rennen über Druck von Ogura – er war direkt hinter mir. Wir hatten heute in den Linkskurven starkes Chattering – das war das Problem. Das war auch schon über das Wochenende so. Auch im Sprint-Rennen am Samstag hat dieses Problem zugenommen. Und doch war ich bester KTM-Pilot, wir haben also einen guten Job gemacht.» Bastianini gestand: «Meine Fahrt war etwas nervös, ich versuche sehr verbissen, um das Podium zu kämpfen. Ich bin schon etwas näher dran jetzt, aber es kommt einfach nicht. Wir haben jetzt noch zwei Chancen – ich will mein Team damit belohnen. In einem Teil des Rennens wollte ich ruhig bleiben und die Reifen schonen. Aber dann hat Marc die Pace hochgeschraubt und ich wollte mitziehen. Aber seine Pace war besser als meine.» Vor den letzten beiden Events und vier Rennen liegt Enea Bastianini auf WM-Rang 10, direkt hinter dem frisch verletzten Ducati-Werksfahrer Pecco Bagnaia. Souveräner Sieg! signals.title: Marc Marquez (2.) in Katar ohne Siegchance: «Mein Rennen war gegen Martin»
signals.summary: Marc Marquez wurde beim Katar-GP Zweiter hinter Aprilia-Ass Marco Bezzecchi. Die Titelparty musste er vertagen. Der Lenovo-Ducati-Pilot fuhr ein schlaues Rennen und ging keine unnötigen Risiken ein. Am Samstag hatte Marc Marquez im turbulenten Katar-Sprint alles richtig gemacht. Nach Abbruch und Neustart setzte er sich gegen Marco Bezzecchi durch, der nach einer Berührung mit dem Spanier stürzte, und feierte seinen 25. Sprintsieg. Mit 49 Punkten Vorsprung auf Jorge Martin ging der Ducati-Werksfahrer in den Grand Prix. Konnte er schon am Sonntagabend feiern? Nur mit einem Sieg – und nur, wenn Martin ohne Punkte bliebe. Marquez erwischte von Position 2 einen starken Start, doch an Polesetter Bezzecchi ging kein Weg vorbei. Raul Fernandez überraschte und überholte den siebenfachen MotoGP-Weltmeister. Während die beiden Aprilia davonzogen, ging Marquez auf Rang 3 kein Risiko ein. Pedro Acosta hängte sich an sein Hinterrad und schnappte sich den Weltmeister in Kurve 15. Kurz darauf ließ der KTM-Pilot Marquez mit einem Fingerzeig demonstrativ wieder vorbei – wie schon in Mandalika. Der Grund: Wieder einmal der Reifendruck. Danach drehte Marquez auf. Mit hohen 1:52er-Rundenzeiten war er zeitweise der Schnellste auf der Strecke und nahm Fernandez mehrere Zehntel pro Runde ab. In der Schlussphase zog er auf der Start-Ziel-Geradem scheinbar mühelos am Trackhouse-Piloten vorbei. An Bezzecchi kam Marquez nicht mehr heran, der Italiener siegte mit drei Sekunden Vorsprung. «Heute war meine Strategie sehr clever. Ich wollte einfach das Rennen managen», erklärte Marquez. «In den ersten fünf Runden war es egal, ob jemand wegfährt. Mein Rennen war vor allem gegen Martin.» Acosta habe ihn wegen eines Reifendruckproblems vorbeigelassen. «Ich habe gesehen, dass ich in dieser Phase des Rennens noch schneller fahren konnte, aber ich wusste, dass ich mit diesem Fahrstil den Vorderreifen zerstöre. Am Ende war Platz 3 okay, aber ich habe gesehen, dass Fernandez Probleme bekam. Man weiß nie – also habe ich angegriffen. Vier Punkte mehr.» Weil Martin als Siebter neun Punkte holte, führt Marquez nun mit 431 Punkten und 60 Zählern Vorsprung, Bezzecchi liegt 74 Punkte zurück. In Portugal hat Marquez den zweiten Matchball. Nach dem Portimao-Sprint sind nur noch 62 Punkte zu vergeben. Gewinnt Marquez den Sprint, ist er Weltmeister, egal was das Aprilia-Duo erreicht. Als Zweiter reicht es, solange Martin den Sprint nicht gewinnt. Souveräner Sieg! signals.summary: Im MotoGP-Grand-Prix in Katar zeigte Marco Bezzecchi eine perfekte Leistung. Er feierte einen Start-Ziel-Sieg vor Marc Marquez und Raul Fernandez. «Es war die Leistung, die wir verdient hatten!» Nach dem Crash im MotoGP-Sprint in Katar war Marco Bezzecchi im Grand Prix am Sonntag auf Revanche aus. Dementsprechend motiviert ging der Aprilia-Pilot ans Werk. Im Rennen über 22 Runden erwischte er einen perfekten Start. «Bez» und Raul Fernandez (Trackhouse) konnten sich rasch vom Rest des Feldes absetzen – in Runde 8 betrug sein Vorsprung bereits über vier Sekunden. Als MM93 nach der Hälfte des Rennens das Tempo angezogen hatte und im 13. Umlauf die schnellste Rennrunde fuhr, reagierte Bezzecchi sofort und fuhr ebenfalls schneller. Marquez machte dann Jagd auf Fernandez, drei Runden vor Schluss ging der Champion an seinem Landsmann vorbei. An der Spitze blieb Bezzecchi cool – er hielt den Abstand konstant und fuhr mit 3,083 sec Vorsprung auf Marquez über die Ziellinie. «Es fühlt sich großartig an, ich bin sehr glücklich. Es war die Leistung, die wir verdient hatten», meinte der Italiener direkt nach dem Rennen im Parc ferme. «Ein großes Dankeschön an das Team und an die Aprilia-Fabrik in Noale. Es war ein fantastisches Wochenende für uns – ich war sehr schnell und habe mich auf dem Motorrad sehr wohl gefühlt.» Bezzecchi ging auch noch einmal auf das Desaster vom Vortag ein, als er im Sprint mit Marc Marquez zusammenstieß und stürzte. «Schade für gestern, aber das ist Teil des Spiels. Auf Teamkollege Jorge Martin fehlen ihm jedoch nur 14 Zähler. In Portimao hat Marquez dann seinen nächsten Matchball im Titelkampf. Souveräner Sieg! signals.summary: Nachdem Joan Mir (Honda) für das MotoGP-Event in Katar absagen musste und Jake Dixon als Ersatzfahrer einspringt, fällt nun auch noch Luca Marini für den Grand Prix aus. Rang im Sprintrennen am Samstag, musste der Italiener für den Grand Prix krankheitsbedingt absagen. «Aufgrund seiner anhaltenden Erschöpfung haben Luca Marini und das Honda-HRC-Castrol-Team beschlossen, ihn vom Katar-GP zurückzuziehen, um sich auf die letzten beiden Rennen der MotoGP-Weltmeisterschaft 2026 zu konzentrieren», hieß es in einem kurzen Statement von HRC. In Malaysia war Marini dann wieder dabei und belegte im Grand Prix am Sonntag den starken siebten Rang. Nun ist er wieder erkrankt. Somit ruhen die Hoffnungen des Honda-Werksteams im Grand Prix in Doha auf Superbike-Ass Jake Dixon. Der Brite springt in Doha für Joan Mir ein. signals.title: Pecco Bagnaia: Kein böses Wort gegen Aldeguer – Blick nach vorne gerichtet
signals.summary: Nach seinem Crash im MotoGP-Sprint in Katar meldete sich Pecco Bagnaia zu Wort. Trotz Knochenbrüchen bleibt der Ducati-Pilot positiv. «Wir hatten viel zu lange mit Frustration zu kämpfen!» Pecco Bagnaia zeigte beim Großen Preis von Katar ein starkes Wochenende. Auf einer seiner Lieblingsstrecken hatte er mit seiner Ducati Desmosedici seit langer Zeit endlich wieder ein gutes Gefühl – in den Trainingssessions und im Qualifying war er bei den schnellsten Fahrern dabei. Dann folgte am Samstag die Katastrophe im MotoGP-Sprint, wo er in der ersten Runde auf Position 5 liegend von Markenkollege Fermin Aldeguer abgeräumt wurde. Bagnaia erlitt bei dem Crash zwei Frakturen an seinem rechten Fuß und mehrere Prellungen am gesamten Körper. Noch in der Nacht von Samstag auf Sonntag wurde er nach Italien ausgeflogen, wo er operiert wird. Mittlerweile meldete sich Bagnaia auf Social Media zu Wort. «Es fühlt sich seltsam an, das zu sagen, aber Katar war für mich tatsächlich eines der besten Wochenenden der Saison. Leider läuft es manchmal nicht so, wie man es sich wünscht, egal wie sehr man sich auch bemüht, das Blatt zu wenden – dagegen kann man nichts tun», so der zweifache MotoGP-Weltmeister. «Es tut mir wirklich leid, aber ich möchte das Positive aus diesem Wochenende mitnehmen, denn wir hatten viel zu lange mit Frustration zu kämpfen. Vielen Dank an euch alle für eure Nachrichten. Mir geht es gut.» In Richtung von Unfallverursacher Fermin Aldeguer gab es kein böses Wort. Der Gresini-Pilot wiederum entschuldigte sich nach dem Rennen bei Bagnaia und dem Ducati-Lenovo-Team für seinen Fehler . Mit dem folgenschweren Sturz in Katar wurde Pecco womöglich die Chance genommen, das gemeinsame Karriere-Kapitel mit Ducati mit Erfolgserlebnissen auf der Rennstrecke zu beenden. Ob der 29-Jährige in zwei Wochen in Portimao und beim Saisonfinale in Valencia dabei sein wird können, ist derzeit ungewiss. Auch sein erster Test mit der 850er-Aprilia am 1. Dezember ist in Gefahr. Aufgrund der Verletzung musste der Gresini-Ducati-Pilot die Grands Prix in Australien und Malaysia auslassen. An diesem Wochenende steht er in Katar wieder am Start. Nach einem verhaltenen Beginn am Freitag, wo Aldeguer im Zeittraining den direkten Einzug ins Q2 verpasste, zeigte er am Samstag im Qualifying eine passable Leistung: Im Q1 fuhr er die schnellste Zeit, womit er sich den Aufstieg in die nächste Qualifying-Session sicherte. In dieser stellte er seine hellblaue Desmosedici auf Startplatz 9. In der ersten Runde des MotoGP-Sprints folgte dann das Desaster. In Kurve 16 bremste Aldeguer viel zu spät und krachte mit seinem Motorrad in das Heck der Ducati von Pecco Bagnaia. Der Italiener flog in hohem Bogen durch die Luft und schlug mit dem Rücken hart auf den Asphalt auf. Danach wurde das Rennen abgebrochen. Bagnaia war zwar bei Bewusstsein, er hatte aber Schmerzen. Es war offensichtlich, dass der Ducati-Werksfahrer den Crash nicht ohne Verletzungen überstanden hatte. Die ersten Untersuchungen im medizinischen Zentrum auf der Rennstrecke ergaben zwei Frakturen an seinem rechten Fuß, die den vierten und fünften Mittelfußknochen betreffen. Zudem hat er mehrere Prellungen am gesamten Körper erlitten. Noch in der Nacht von Samstag auf Sonntag wurde Bagnaia nach Italien ausgeflogen. Aldeguer war sich darüber bewusst, dass er einen folgenschweren Fehler gemacht hatte. «Ich möchte mich bei Pecco und seinem gesamten Team entschuldigen. Ich habe bei einem Überholversuch einen Fehler gemacht, und das tut mir wirklich leid», meinte der 21-Jährige. Der Zwischenfall blieb auch für Aldeguer nicht ohne Folgen. Nach dem Neustart des auf zehn Runden verkürzten Sprintrennens musste er eine doppelte Long-lap absolvieren. Bis zur vierten Runde kämpfte sich der Spanier auf Rang 7 nach vorn. Dann folgte die erste Long-lap – nach dieser war er Zwölfter. Nachdem er seinen zweiten Umweg absolvierte hatte, behielt er diese Position. In der letzten Runde konnte Aldeguer dann noch an KTM-Pilot Brad Binder vorbeigehen – er überquerte die Ziellinie als Elfter, mit 9,429 sec Rückstand auf Sieger Marc Marquez. «Die doppelte Long-lap-Strafe hat uns nicht ausgebremst, wir hatten eine gute Pace. Am Sonntag werden wir versuchen, wieder zurückzukommen. Noch einmal: Ich entschuldige mich bei Pecco», so Fermin Aldeguer. signals.title: Johann Zarco (Honda) fürchtete sich vor einem dunklen MotoGP-Schatten
signals.summary: LCR-Honda-Pilot Johann Zarco meisterte den Wüstensprint in Katar und kam als Fünfter ins Ziel. Der Franzose berichtete von einem super Start, einem guten Rennen und einem furchterregenden Schatten. Nach einem starken Qualifying ging Johann Zarco von Position 7 in das erste kurze Rennen in Katar – und war damit einmal mehr die mit Abstand bestimmende Kraft im Honda-Lager. Abgewunken wurde der routinierte, aber stets hochmotivierte Racer aus Cannes auf Platz 5. Zarco war sich der Geschenke bewusst, konnte aber dennoch selbstbewusst von seinem Auftritt sprechen. «Platz 5 ist ein sehr schönes Ergebnis, auch wenn ich einige Plätze durch Stürze anderer gewonnen habe», so Zarco und sprach damit vom gewaltigen Abflug von Bagnaia und dem ebenfalls nach einer Kollision ausgerutschten Marco Bezzecchi. Beide Konkurrenten lagen zum Zeitpunkt der Abflüge als auch im Q2 vor dem Franzosen auf der Kunden-Honda. Zarco weiter: «Ich habe sicherlich auch profitiert von dem Abbruch. Es hat mir geholfen, denn der erste Start war nicht so gut, der zweite dagegen sehr, sehr gut. Ich bin auch froh, dass es mir gelungen ist, wieder hochkonzentriert neu zu starten. Ich hatte kurz Erinnerungen an Catalunya, aber jetzt, ohne Schmerzen und Adrenalin, war es kein Problem. Mein Tempo zu Beginn war sehr hoch, ich war überrascht, wie gut ich mit den Top 3 mithalten konnte.» «Ich habe dann auch erwogen, «Diggia» für Platz 3 anzugreifen, aber ich wollte auf keinen Fall einen Fehler machen», schilderte der 36-Jährige. Dann wurde es spannend. «Raul hat mich dann in Kurve 12 überholt, dabei musste ich das Bike aufrichten. Direkt danach sah ich einen dunklen Schatten – ich dachte kurz, gleich wird ein anderer Pilot über mich fliegen. Es war Acosta, doch er war weiter weg, als ich dachte, und er hatte alles unter Kontrolle. Nach diesem Schreck mit dem Schatten habe ich etwas Zeit verloren, konnte aber die Position halten. Ich bin happy, fürchte aber, es wird schwer, dort zu fahren, wenn es über die doppelte Distanz geht.» Der Ausblick auf den Großen Preis bereitet dem lange verletzten Honda-Piloten noch kein gutes Gefühl. «In den ersten Runden mit frischen Reifen ist mein Tempo sehr hoch, gut genug, um in den Top 5 zu fahren. Doch der Speed frisst sehr viel Energie, der Hinterreifen wird zu sehr beansprucht und noch habe ich keine Idee, wie das im GP funktionieren soll.» Vor dem drittletzten GP-Rennen der Saison rangiert der Altmeister, bedingt durch das lange Aus, auf dem aussichtslosen 17. Tabellenrang. Zarco liegt neun Punkte hinter Franco Morbidelli, 22 Punkte hinter Teamkollege Moreira und 23 Zähler hinter Landsmann Fabio Quartararo, der in der Wüste von Katar als Yamaha-Athlet nicht am Start ist. Souveräner Sieg! signals.summary: Der Crash im MotoGP-Sprint in Katar ging für Pecco Bagnaia (Ducati) nicht ohne Blessuren aus. Er wurde ins Krankenhaus nach Doha gebracht und wird weiter nach Italien zur Operation transportiert. Endlich lief es bei Pecco Bagnaia mal wieder, da krachte es! Vierter im Zeittraining am Freitag, Fünfter im Qualifying, im Rennen am Samstagabend in der ersten Runde in der letzten Kurve vor der langen Start-Ziel-Geraden von Fermin Aldeguer (Gresini Ducati) auf Position 5 liegend abgeschossen. Der junge Spanier war viel zu spät auf der Bremse, torpedierte Bagnaias Motorrad, woraufhin sich dessen Ducati in sämtliche Teile zerlegend unzählige Male überschlug. Pecco flog auch hoch durch die Luft, schlug hart auf dem Asphalt auf, war aber bei Bewusstsein, als das Rennen abgebrochen wurde und das medizinische Personal zum Italiener geeilt kam. «Die ersten Untersuchungen von Francesco Bagnaia im medizinischen Zentrum des Lusail International Circuit ergaben zwei Frakturen an seinem rechten Fuß, die den vierten und fünften Mittelfußknochen betreffen», teilte der medizinische Direktor der MotoGP, Dr. Angel Charte, direkt nach dem Unfall mit. «Der Fahrer wird zur weiteren Untersuchung in ein Krankenhaus in Doha verlegt, um festzustellen, ob die Frakturen operativ behandelt werden müssen.» Inzwischen ist klar: Für den zweifachen MotoGP-Champion ist der Grand Prix von Katar am Persischen Golf beendet. Der Fuß muss operiert werden, Bagnaia wird in der Nacht von Samstag auf Sonntag nach Italien transportiert und sich dort zu den Ärzten seines Vertrauens begeben. Neben den zwei Brüchen hat er mehrere starke Prellungen am ganzen Körper. Auf seine – ohnehin verkorkste – Weltmeisterschaft hat der Unfall kaum Auswirkungen. Zum vor ihm platzierten Alex Marquez, der in Doha ebenfalls verletzt fehlt , hat er 24 Punkte Rückstand. Und auf den hinter ihm liegenden Enea Bastianini (Red Bull KTM Tech3) 37 Vorsprung. Am Wochenende nach Katar ist rennfrei. Ob Bagnaia in 13 Tagen in Portimao wieder dabei ist, hängt laut Ducati von seinem Genesungsverlauf ab. Aldeguer bekam für sein Vergehen von den FIM MotoGP Stewards zwei Long-Laps für den Neustart des Sprints aufgebrummt, der Spanier wurde dennoch Elfter - 9,429 sec hinter Sieger Marc Marquez (Ducati Lenovo). Souveräner Sieg! signals.title: Acosta zu Bagnaia-Crash: «Die MotoGP hatte lange nicht mehr so einen Sturz»
signals.summary: Im Katar-Sprint der MotoGP auf dem Losail-Circuit kämpfte sich Pedro Acosta aus dem Q1 in die Punkte. Den wilden Crash von Ducati-Pilot Francesco Bagnaia sah der Red Bull-Athlet aus bester Position. Pedro Acosta reiste als einer von vier verbliebenen Titelanwärtern nach Lusail, doch der Freitag verlief zäh. Der KTM-Werksfahrer musste nach Platz 14 im Q1 antreten, wo er sich als Zweiter für doch noch für das wichtige Q2 qualifizierte. Dort bremste ihn erneut ein technisches Problem, am Ende reichte es für Startplatz 8. «Q1 lief nicht übertrieben gut, war aber keine Katastrophe. Im Q2 lief es gut bis zu einem technischen Problem», bilanzierte Acosta. Der erste Start gelang dem 22-Jährigen nach Maß, in Runde 2 setzte er Francesco Bagnaia (Ducati) im Kampf um Rang 5 bereits unter Druck. In der Zielkurve schoss dann Fermin Aldeguer (Gresini-Ducati) innen an Acosta vorbei und räumte Bagnaia ab. Acosta blieb verschont, das Sprintrennen wurde abgebrochen. «Es ist lange her, dass man in der MotoGP so einen Sturz gesehen hat. Ich hoffe, dass es Pecco gut geht», sendete Acosta dem Italiener Genesungswünsche und nahm Aldeguer unter Schutz: «Die Aktion kam sehr früh und aggressiv. Ich verstehe aber seine Lage. Fermin kommt von einer Verletzung zurück. Man muss sich an die Aero und das Bike wieder gewöhnen. Da kann jeder einen Fehler machen.» Nach dem Neustart über zehn Runden wurde Acosta früh von Jorge Martin (Aprilia) überholt, setzte dann Raul Fernandez unter Druck. Als Marco Bezzecchi (Aprilia) ebenfalls aus dem Rennen war, lag der 22-Jährige zeitweise auf Rang 5, doch Johann Zarco (LCR-Honda) schnappte sich den Spanier wieder. Bis ins Ziel hielt Acosta Ai Ogura (Trackhouse-Aprilia) noch hinter sich und wurde Sechster. «Ich habe gelitten, den Reifen zum Arbeiten zu bringen. Wir müssen verstehen, warum, denn das ist mir auch beim Neustart in Barcelona passiert», erklärte Acosta. Er war überzeugt: «Ohne diese rote Flagge hätten wir Möglichkeiten für mehr gehabt. Nicht unbedingt das Podium, aber ein Ergebnis in den Top-4.» In der WM liegt Acosta mit 299 Punkten nun 112 Zähler hinter Marc Marquez. Da im Katar-GP, in Portimao und in Valencia nur noch 99 Punkte zu vergeben sind, ist der KTM-Pilot rechnerisch aus dem Titelrennen. Im Gegensatz zu dem Trainingsfreitag sieht sich Acosta auf einem guten Weg: «Wir haben das Wochenende gedreht, trotzdem sind wir noch weit weg.» Souveräner Sieg! signals.title: Benda’s new Roadster range begins to take shape with pair of V-twins
signals.summary: After debuting a brand-new V-twin-powered adventure bike at EICMA, Benda has rolled out two new Roadster motorcycles using the same platform. The Chinese motorcycle company Benda has just launched two brand-new Roadster models, that while similar in many ways, offer slight differences in their appearance. Like the new Capra 700 adventure bike, which was also unveiled at EICMA, both the Vinster 700 and Vinster X 700 are powered by the same 691.6cc liquid-cooled V2, an engine which they share with the Benda Rock 707, too. The Vinsters will also produce the same 72bhp at 9,000rpm and 50 Ib-ft of torque at 6,500rpm as their new adventure sibling. Additionally, the double-cradle frame, aluminium swingarm, and suspension are all shared between both Vinster models. The front suspension setup features upside-down telescopic forks offering 135mm of travel, while a hydraulic shock produces 120mm of travel at the rear. Two-channel ABS is also found front and rear, with stopping power handled by single discs at both ends of the bike, together with a four-piston caliper (front) and two-piston caliper (rear). Where things begin to differentiate is their style, with the Vinster 700 adopting more of a traditional roadster, while the X model takes on a more touring-inspired look. The Vinster 700 makes use of 17-inch wheels, while the X variant rides on a 19-inch front. Seat height is also different between both models, with Benda claiming 830mm for the Vinster 700, and 865mm for the X. Prior to EICMA 2026 getting underway, Benda confirmed it would be entering three new segments, one of which is the above-mentioned Roadster category. At the heart of its decision to do so was its V2 platform, with Petr Badura, Transportation Designer at Benda Motor Europe, saying: “The Vinster started with a designer’s idea that captured everyone’s imagination. We already had the 700cc V2 engine from our cruiser range, and we began asking ourselves: why not build a roadster around it? From the outset, we wanted to create a contrast between carefully sculpted bodywork and the raw, mechanical character of the V2. “The engine is the heart of the motorcycle, and rather than hiding it away, we wanted to celebrate it. signals.title: I ain’t gettin’ on no plane! Why the new Fireblade standard and SP are without wings
signals.summary: Winglets might be fashionable, but Honda says they're not necessary on every Fireblade. Here's why the 2027 standard and SP models go without them. Winglets have become almost obligatory on modern superbikes, but Honda has taken a slightly different approach with its 2027 CBR1000RR-R Fireblade, offering its standard and SP models without the aerodynamic appendages. The Japanese manufacturer has reserved the prominent winglets for its range-topping HRC Works Edition, leaving the other two versions with a cleaner-looking front end. According to Takazumi Hayashi, the decision comes down to the different priorities of the three motorcycles. Speaking to Visordown at EICMA 2026, the Fireblade's Large Project Leader explained that the HRC Works Edition was developed with racing performance as its primary objective, with its aerodynamic package generating significantly more downforce than the standard and SP versions. Hayashi put that difference at around 3.5 times the downforce, although the additional aerodynamic performance comes with a compromise. The extra equipment adds a tad more weight to the bike and can have an impact on handling, which is why Honda decided to develop the standard and SP versions without the same aerodynamic package. "To improve handling, we developed the standard and SP versions," Hayashi explained. He added that the two models are lighter and offer different handling characteristics to the HRC Works Edition. Interestingly, Hayashi admitted that he personally prefers the appearance of the Fireblade without winglets, although he was clear that their use remains important for racing. "For racing performance and to comply with current regulations, winglets are indispensable," he said. "We cannot eliminate them from the racing version." So, Honda's decision to ditch them from two bikes in the Fireblade family isn't the brand suggesting that winglets are pointless, or that its standard and SP models achieve identical aerodynamic performance without them. Instead, it has chosen to give its customers a choice between a more road-focused configuration and a version developed with racing firmly in mind. The decision also appears to have been made without any major disagreement between Honda's engineering and marketing departments. Hayashi explained that both sides understood the thinking behind the three-model range from the beginning, with the HRC Works Edition aimed at racing, while the standard and SP versions are intended for riders who want to enjoy their Fireblade on the road and on public roads. signals.title: Honda RN0 debuts as the motorcycle manufacturer’s first e-MTB model
signals.summary: After producing its first motor-assisted bicycle 80 years ago, Honda has now entered the e-MTB space for the first time. After revealing a prototype model in September, Honda has moved swiftly to launch its first-ever e-MTB machine at EICMA. Officially called RN0, the new electric mountain bike marks a major milestone for the marque, which produced its first motor-assisted bicycle in 1946. This was through a project named ‘Batabata’, which ultimately began the Japanese company’s journey to becoming the world’s largest motorcycle manufacturer. Since 1946, there have been numerous projects launched by Honda in the powered bicycle space, including the electric-assisted Raccoon model, which was then followed by the 1996 Raccoon CX featuring MTB styling. However, the new RN0 is the latest, and arguably the most significant electric model it has produced outside of the WN7 motorcycle, of course. It has been developed in collaboration with e-MTB manufacturer ROTWILD, and was guided by Large Project Leader Yusuke Muto, a lifelong cycling enthusiast whose involvement in mountain biking dates back to 1995. At the heart of the new e-MTB machine is a Shimano drive unit producing 100 Nm (around 73 Ib-ft) of torque and 750W of power. The bike’s torque and power figures are fed by a removable 720Wh battery, meanwhile, the 12-speed Shimano Deore XT Di2 drivetrain enables Shimano’s Auto Shift and Auto Assist technology functions to operate smoothly when selecting gears. Additionally, the RN0 features a motorcycle-inspired carbon monocoque frame that’s paired with Honda's distinctive Gullwing swingarm and linkage system. Suspension duties are handled by Fox Float Factory Kashima forks and a Fox rear shock, while the RN0 also makes use of Shimano XT brakes and DT-Swiss H1900 wheels (29-inch front and 27.5-inch rear) wrapped in Schwalbe tyres. Key information is displayed across a 2.2-inch display integrated into the top tube, while a USB-C charging port allows riders to keep devices powered on the move. Furthermore, the Shimano CONNECT mobile app, once downloaded, can be used as a cycle computer, giving riders the option to lock and unlock the bike's electronic systems for greater security. signals.title: Seized motorcycle collection featuring MotoGP bikes is heading for sale
signals.summary: A $40m motorcycle collection amassed by former Olympian turned drug kingpin, Ryan Wedding, is set to go under the hammer. A seized motorcycle collection believed to be worth around $40m, which includes rare MotoGP and WorldSBK machines as well as rare road bikes, is set to go up for auction. The collection belonged to ex-Olympian snowboarder Ryan Wedding, who was arrested in connection to running a multi-million dollar drug trafficking operation. Wedding was arrested in Mexico and transferred to the United States to face federal charges in January of this year. At the time of his arrest, the FBI said he was apprehended following cooperation with Mexican authorities after years of being a fugitive. According to US authorities, Wedding was accused of running a cocaine trafficking network linked to the Sinaloa Cartel, while charges connected to organised crime and multiple drug-related murders, including the killing of a federal witness, were also announced. Aside from his connections to drug trafficking, Wedding amassed a rare motorcycle collection featuring some of the world’s most impressive bikes. Numerous grand prix machines form part of the collection, including bikes ridden by Valentino Rossi, Marc Marquez, Andrea Dovizioso and Jorge Lorenzo. A total of 61 motorcycles are believed to be included in the collection, with models from Ducati, Honda, Kawasaki, MV Agusta, Suzuki and Yamaha all featured. The motorcycle collection was discovered during raids in the Mexican capital and the nearby Mexico state last December at addresses linked to Wedding, who was one of the FBI's most wanted fugitives at the time. Wedding’s arrest was a top priority to US authorities, so much so, a $15 million reward had been offered for information leading to his capture. In terms of the motorcycle collection, around 10 to 15 bikes are thought to be MotoGP prototypes and WorldSBK-spec machines. The Institute to Return the Stolen to the People (INDEP) will auction the motorcycle collection on November 11, with bids starting at around 1,600 US dollars (around £1,200). signals.title: Motorcyclists face parking restrictions while Lime Bikes get a free ride, but that could be about to change
signals.summary: Motorcyclists face strict parking rules, but dockless hire e-bikes have often been left blocking pavements. New Government proposals could change that. Britain's pavements could soon become a little less cluttered, with the Government proposing new powers to tackle the growing problem of poorly parked hire e-bikes. The plans could be particularly interesting for motorcyclists, who have long had to navigate increasingly restrictive parking rules while fleets of relatively heavy electric hire bikes have apparently got a free pass to be left scattered across public footpaths. The Department for Transport (DfT) launched a consultation on November 5, 2026, setting out proposals for national standards covering shared cycle schemes operated by companies including Lime, Voi, Forest, Beryl, Dott and Bolt. Under the proposals, local authorities would gain powers to licence operators and establish minimum standards for how their fleets are managed. That could include designated parking arrangements, restrictions on fleet sizes and operating areas, and requirements for companies to maintain their bikes in a safe condition. There are also plans to tackle antisocial behaviour, including riding on pavements, cycling under the influence and allowing underage users to access hire bikes. Authorities could introduce clear consequences for those caught breaking the rules, including fines. For motorcyclists, that will be welcome news, and points to the days of having to find a dedicated parking space, while hire scheme e-bikes litter the pavement, are coming to an end. Depending on where you live, finding somewhere to legally park a motorcycle can already be something of a lottery, with restrictions on pavement parking and designated motorcycle bays varying between local authorities. Meanwhile, dockless hire bikes have become a familiar sight abandoned across pavements, sometimes obstructing pedestrian routes, dropped kerbs and access for wheelchair users. Their considerable weight also makes them far from harmless obstacles, particularly for people with impaired vision or mobility. The proposals also include the possibility of insurance requirements for operators, potentially making it easier for pedestrians to claim compensation if they are injured in a collision involving a shared e-bike. Importantly, these are proposals rather than rules that have already come into force. The consultation will run until December 31, 2026, with the Government looking to establish a more consistent framework across England. signals.title: Brent crude crashes but UK diesel remains close to £2 a litre
signals.summary: Oil prices are falling, but UK motorists are still paying nearly £2 a litre for diesel. Why aren't pump prices coming down? British motorists could be forgiven for wondering when they will see the benefit of falling oil prices, with Brent crude dropping sharply this week while fuel prices at UK forecourts remain stubbornly high. The international oil benchmark fell by 8.7 per cent on Wednesday, 4 November, dropping below $95 a barrel for the first time in two months. That followed the US mid-term elections, which saw Donald Trump's Republicans lose control of Congress to the Democrats, prompting financial markets to reassess the likelihood of an end to the conflict between the US, Israel and Iran. The prospect of de-escalation in the Middle East has reduced some of the geopolitical risk premium previously built into oil prices, with traders increasingly optimistic that a diplomatic solution could ease pressure on global oil supplies. For context, Brent crude closed at $117.64 a barrel on 30 October. By Wednesday, it had fallen to $94.62, representing a drop of almost 20 per cent in just a few days. Although prices recovered to around $99.58 on Friday morning following renewed concerns over shipping security in the Gulf, the benchmark remains significantly below its recent highs. That same enthusiasm is yet to translate into meaningful savings for British motorists, though, as both petrol and diesel prices remain cripplingly high. According to the latest figures from the UK Fuel Price Index published by PetrolPrices.co.uk, the average price of unleaded petrol stood at 172.78p per litre for the week ending 2 November, while diesel was averaging 198.58p. More recent daily figures show some movement, with petrol averaging around 170.6p and diesel 198.3p on 6 November. That is a modest improvement, but hardly the sort of reduction motorists might expect when international oil prices have fallen so sharply. There are several reasons why movements in crude oil prices don't immediately translate into changes at the pumps. Firstly, crude oil is not the same product as the petrol and diesel sold at forecourts. It has to be refined, transported, blended and distributed before reaching retailers. The wholesale prices of finished petrol and diesel are therefore influenced by factors beyond the price of Brent crude, including refining capacity, global demand, supply availability and the cost of biofuel blending, which is effectively turning pure petrol into an ethanol blend. The exchange rate also matters. Refined fuel is traded internationally in US dollars, meaning a weaker pound can eat into any savings generated by falling oil prices. There is also a time delay. According to the RAC, it typically takes around two weeks for changes in wholesale fuel costs to work their way through the supply chain and be reflected in forecourt prices. That means motorists shouldn't necessarily expect to see the full benefit of this week's oil price movement immediately. Then there is taxation. UK motorists currently pay 57.95p per litre in fuel duty, with VAT charged at 20 per cent on the final price, including fuel duty. Consequently, a substantial proportion of every litre purchased goes directly to the Treasury rather than towards the cost of the fuel itself. However, while those factors help explain why pump prices don't move in lockstep with crude oil, they don't necessarily explain why reductions can appear to trickle down to consumers so slowly. The speed at which fuel prices increase compared with how slowly they fall has been a long-running source of frustration for motorists. FairFuelUK has now put fuel retailers on notice following Brent crude's latest decline, calling on supermarkets, oil companies and independent forecourts to pass on lower wholesale costs as quickly as market conditions allow. Founder Howard Cox said: "Oil has crashed. So the clock starts now." He added that motorists should expect the same urgency when international oil and wholesale prices fall as they experience when those costs rise. FairFuelUK says it will monitor petrol and diesel prices over the next seven, 14, 21 and 28 days to establish how quickly any reductions reach forecourts. The organisation is also renewing its calls for a PumpWatch system, which would provide greater transparency over the relationship between international oil prices, wholesale fuel costs, retailer margins and the prices motorists ultimately pay.
